flagged.urlStatus: Loaded and supports the explanation: it lists 'Automatically recover from failure' and 'Test recovery procedures' as reliability design principles.
flagged.evidence: "There are five design principles for reliability in the cloud: Automatically recover from failure ... Test recovery procedures ..." (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/rel-dp.html)
flagged.problem: The answer (false) and the explanation are correct, but the statement is a strawman. Nobody who knows the pillar names would think cost optimization exists to recover from failures, because the name alone gives it away, so the card teaches almost nothing.
flagged.suggestedFix: Make the distractor a pillar a learner could plausibly mix up with reliability, and test a named principle. For example: "'Automatically recover from failure' is a design principle of the performance efficiency pillar." Answer: false. Explanation: "Automatically recover from failure is one of the five reliability design principles, along with testing recovery procedures and scaling horizontally." Keep the rel-dp.html source.

flagged.evidence: "Cloud computing lets you focus on your own customers, rather than on the heavy lifting of racking, stacking, and powering servers." https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-overview/six-advantages-of-cloud-computing.html
flagged.problem: The fact is correct, but the true statement is close to self-evident (of course you pay to power your own servers). It tests no real misconception. The useful idea, that on-premises TCO goes beyond the hardware price, is only in the explanation.
flagged.suggestedFix: Make it test the misconception: "When you compare on-premises costs with AWS, only the server hardware purchase price needs to be counted." Answer: false. Explanation: On-premises total cost of ownership also includes ongoing costs such as power, cooling, data center space, and the labor to rack, stack, and maintain servers. AWS takes on these costs as part of its service.

flagged.evidence: "Through effective automation, you can achieve consistent responses to events, limit human error, and reduce operator toil." https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/oe-design-principles.html
flagged.problem: The statement is a tautology: automating a manual task obviously reduces the manual work for it. It is not specific to AWS or cloud economics, and nobody would answer false. The explanation is accurate.
flagged.suggestedFix: Tie it to AWS automation and its economic benefit, for example: "Defining infrastructure as code with AWS CloudFormation lets teams provision environments consistently and repeatably, which reduces operational effort and human error." Answer: true. Or as a false statement: "Automating infrastructure provisioning on AWS increases the risk of configuration errors compared with manual setup." Answer: false.

flagged.urlStatus: Loaded. The page covers the general idea ("Measure overall efficiency") but does not mention cost per transaction or the arithmetic.
flagged.evidence: "Measure overall efficiency: Measure the business output of the workload and the costs associated with delivery. Use this data to understand the gains you make from increasing output, increasing functionality, and reducing cost." https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/cost-optimization-pillar/design-principles.html
flagged.problem: The statement is pure arithmetic: if the numerator (spend) grows more slowly than the denominator (transactions), the ratio falls. It is true by definition, not specific to AWS, and teaches no cloud economics concept. Unit-cost metrics are also at the edge of CLF scope.
flagged.suggestedFix: drop, or rewrite toward the AWS principle: "The AWS Well-Architected cost optimization guidance recommends measuring the business output of a workload together with its delivery costs, not just total spend." Answer: true.
